I’m sorry your husband is living with such a serious disability. The neurologist’s observation and the records from both hospitals give a malpractice attorney a concrete basis to investigate. The key question is not only whether the first ER missed the stroke, but **whether recognizing it that evening would likely have prevented or reduced his lasting disability**.

**Filing deadline.** Based on the first ER visit being about four months ago, a claim against the private Queens hospital appears to be within New York’s ordinary **2 years and 6 months** under CPLR §214-a, measured from the alleged error. Continuous treatment for the same condition can move the start to the last treatment in that course, but a visit to a different hospital the next morning ordinarily does not extend the deadline against the first ER. The foreign-object discovery rule, Lavern’s Law for missed cancer, and the infancy toll under CPLR §208 don’t appear to apply.

The hospital’s private status makes a public-hospital deadline unlikely, but counsel should confirm who employed the clinicians. If a city or county entity was involved, the **90-day notice-of-claim deadline** under General Municipal Law §50-e may already have passed, and the usual lawsuit deadline is one year and 90 days. If a clinician was federally covered, a written administrative claim generally must be presented to the responsible agency within **two years** of when your husband knew or should have known of the injury and its cause.

**Standard of care and causation.** Sudden slurred speech and one-sided facial droop should prompt a reasonably competent emergency clinician to evaluate for stroke urgently, establish when your husband was last known to be well, and obtain prompt brain imaging, typically a noncontrast CT to check for bleeding. If the first ER discharged him with a migraine diagnosis without an appropriate stroke evaluation, that is a serious potential departure from the standard of care. An early CT can be normal in an ischemic stroke, so the question is broader than whether a scan would have shown a stroke.

An emergency medicine or stroke expert should reconstruct the timeline from the triage notes, neurologic exams, and imaging. The fact that it was too late for a clot-busting drug the next morning **doesn’t by itself establish that he was eligible the night before**. An expert would assess whether he had an ischemic stroke, whether he qualified for clot-busting medication or a clot-removal procedure at the time, and whether timely treatment likely would have reduced the weakness that now limits his mobility.

*Hackshaw v. Mercy Medical Center*, 139 A.D.3d 798; 33 N.Y.S.3d 297, is a related New York appellate malpractice decision; the available excerpt does not establish a stroke-specific rule. I’d bring both hospitals’ records to a New York malpractice attorney promptly, including any ambulance records and the actual scan images if you have them. Counsel can verify the deadlines and arrange the expert review generally required for the certificate of merit under CPLR §3012-a.

This is general information, not legal advice.

I’m sorry your mother died, and that the hospital left your family without an explanation. The fever and high white blood cell count at discharge, followed two days later by septic shock, warrant prompt review by a medical malpractice attorney. The second doctor’s comment is an important lead, but an expert would need to review the records to determine whether the discharge fell below the standard of care and whether earlier diagnosis or treatment would likely have prevented her death.

**Deadlines.** Under EPTL § 5-4.1, the wrongful death action generally must be started within **two years of your mother’s death**. At seven weeks, you are still well within that period. But Kings County Hospital is part of NYC Health + Hospitals, so the shorter **notice-of-claim deadline** is urgent. Under GML § 50-e, the wrongful death notice generally must be served within **90 days of the estate representative’s formal appointment**. The survival claim can have a separate notice deadline that may run from the malpractice rather than the appointment, as well as its own filing deadline under CPLR § 214-a and applicable public-hospital rules. Don’t wait for the hospital’s explanation before having counsel check those dates.

**Your authority to act.** Being named executor in the will is not the same as being appointed. If Surrogate’s Court has issued **Letters Testamentary**, you generally can act as the estate’s personal representative. If it hasn’t, you’ll generally need to obtain them. Either way, a lawyer can check the notice deadlines now.

**Potential damages.** Under EPTL § 5-4.3, wrongful death damages can include the financial support and household services your mother would have provided to eligible family members, as well as qualifying medical and funeral expenses. New York does not compensate survivors for grief or loss of companionship. Separately, under EPTL § 11-3.2, the estate may recover for **your mother’s own conscious pain and suffering** before death if the evidence shows she was conscious and suffering. Family observations, ambulance records, and hospital notes may help establish that.

A related New York malpractice decision is *Hackshaw v. Mercy Medical Center*, 139 A.D.3d 798; 33 N.Y.S.3d 297. For your family, the most useful next step is to speak promptly with a New York malpractice attorney who handles NYC Health + Hospitals claims. Have the exact dates of discharge, readmission, death, and any court appointment ready, along with any discharge papers you have.

This is general information, not legal advice.

The hospital nurse’s observation is an important lead, but the records and an expert review would help determine whether the nursing home failed to prevent or treat the sores and whether an infection from those wounds contributed to his death.

- **Wrongful death deadline.** Under EPTL §5-4.1, the usual deadline is two years from the date of death. At five months, you appear to have about 19 months left under that rule. Don’t wait for the estate appointment to start checking deadlines: if a city- or county-run facility was involved, GML §50-e generally requires a wrongful death notice of claim within 90 days of the representative’s appointment, and separate deadlines can apply to the survival claim.
- **Estate appointment.** Being his only son does not automatically authorize you to sue. If your father had no will, you can generally petition the Surrogate’s Court in the county where he was domiciled to appoint you as administrator. If he had a will, the named executor ordinarily seeks appointment. The court-appointed personal representative brings the claims.
- **Potential damages.** Under EPTL §5-4.3, wrongful death damages can include the financial support and household services your father would likely have provided to eligible family members, as well as qualifying medical and funeral expenses. New York does not compensate survivors for grief or loss of companionship. Separately, under EPTL §11-3.2, the estate may recover for your father’s own conscious pain and suffering before death if the evidence supports it. If that claim sounds in medical malpractice, CPLR §214-a generally runs two years and six months from the alleged malpractice or the end of qualifying continuous treatment—not from the date of death.

A related New York malpractice decision is *Manswell v. Montefiore Medical Center*, 2016 NY Slip Op 7855; 144 A.D.3d 564; 42 N.Y.S.3d 13. For your father’s case, a New York nursing-home malpractice attorney can help you start the appointment process, verify both deadlines, and request the nursing home’s skin assessments, repositioning and wound-care records, along with the hospital’s records on the source of the sepsis.
